lead: A continuous-wave radar transmits all the time and never times a pulse. It listens for the small frequency shift that a moving target puts on the echo: the Doppler shift. That gives speed only. Sweep the transmit frequency linearly and the echo arrives with a delay, so mixing echo and reference produces a beat frequency proportional to range. This is FMCW radar, used in aircraft radio altimeters, tank level gauges and cheap intruder sensors.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for the radar block diagram, and Unit 5 for mixer operation and oscillator phase noise.

blocks.text: A CW radar has one oscillator running continuously at f<sub>0</sub>. The transmit antenna radiates a pure tone and a separate receive antenna collects the echo; separate antennas keep the strong transmitter from saturating the receiver. For a stationary target the echo has the same frequency. For a target moving toward or away from the radar, the echo frequency shifts by the Doppler frequency:

blocks.where: f<sub>d</sub> is the Doppler frequency in Hz; v<sub>r</sub> is the radial velocity in m/s, positive for a closing target; λ = c / f<sub>0</sub> is the wavelength in m.

blocks.text: A mixer multiplies the echo with a sample of the transmitter. The output has a sum term near 2f<sub>0</sub> and a difference term at f<sub>d</sub>; a low-pass Doppler filter keeps only f<sub>d</sub>, and a counter or FFT shows it. A closing target gives positive f<sub>d</sub> and a higher echo frequency. An opening target gives negative f<sub>d</sub>.

A single-frequency CW radar has no timing mark on the transmitted wave, so it cannot measure range. It also cannot see a stationary target, whose f<sub>d</sub> is zero, and it cannot separate two closing targets at different ranges if their radial speeds are equal: both produce one Doppler tone. It is a speed sensor, not a range sensor.

sections.h3: FMCW: add a sweep, get range

blocks.text: FMCW radar sweeps the oscillator frequency in a sawtooth from f<sub>0</sub> to f<sub>0</sub>+Δf over a sweep period T<sub>m</sub>, then repeats. The echo from a target at range R comes back after delay τ = 2R/c. By then the oscillator has moved on, so the echo frequency differs from the current transmit frequency. The mixer multiplies the echo with a sample of the current sweep and produces a low beat frequency f<sub>b</sub>. During the delay τ the sweep has advanced by Δf(τ/T<sub>m</sub>), so

blocks.where: f<sub>b</sub> is the beat frequency in Hz; R is range in m; Δf is the sweep bandwidth in Hz; T<sub>m</sub> is the sweep period in s; c = 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s.

blocks.text: The beat is constant during the ramp; counting it gives range. Range resolution is set by sweep bandwidth:

blocks.where: ΔR is the range resolution in m; Δf is the sweep bandwidth in Hz.

blocks.text: A larger Δf gives finer range bins. Maximum range is limited by the largest beat frequency the receiver and ADC can handle, and by the sampling rate; it is not limited by pulse repetition frequency because there is no pulse. Triangular modulation uses an up-ramp and a down-ramp. A moving target adds the Doppler shift to the beat: the up and down beat frequencies differ by 2f<sub>d</sub>, so averaging them gives range and their difference gives radial speed.

sections.h3: Multiple tones and where this is used

blocks.text: Two or more CW tones can give range without a sweep. Transmit f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub>, receive both echoes, and measure the phase of each. The round-trip phase is φ = 4πR/λ, so the phase difference between the tones changes with R. The range is unambiguous up to R<sub>max</sub> = c / (2 Δf), where Δf is the spacing between the two tones in Hz; wider spacing gives a shorter unambiguous range. Only a few universities teach this as multiple-frequency radar.

Applications follow directly. A police speed gun is CW: it reads f<sub>d</sub>. A radio altimeter is FMCW: it reads f<sub>b</sub> downward to the ground. A tank level gauge is usually FMCW: it measures surface distance from f<sub>b</sub>. A CW version can only flag that the surface has reached a set level, not how far away it is. A proximity fuse and an intruder sensor use the same Doppler or beat signal.

figure.caption: The swept oscillator feeds both the transmit antenna and the mixer reference; the delayed echo mixed with that reference gives the beat frequency, so counting f<sub>b</sub> gives range R.

spec.title: FMCW radar
spec.aria: FMCW radar: a swept oscillator feeds the transmit antenna and also the mixer reference, and the delayed echo mixed with that reference gives a beat frequency proportional to range.

examples.question: (a) A police CW radar works at 10.525 GHz. A car approaches at 100 km/h. Find the wavelength and the Doppler frequency. (b) An FMCW radio altimeter has sweep bandwidth Δf = 100 MHz and sweep period T<sub>m</sub> = 1 ms. Find the beat frequency for ground at range R = 150 m. Take c = 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s.
steps: v<sub>r</sub> = 100 / 3.6 = 27.78 m/s. The car is closing, so v<sub>r</sub> is positive.
f<sub>d</sub> = 2 v<sub>r</sub> / λ = (2 × 27.78) / 0.0285 = 1949 Hz. This is about 1.95 kHz.
examples.answer: λ = 0.0285 m, f<sub>d</sub> = 1949 Hz, and f<sub>b</sub> = 100000 Hz (100 kHz).
examples.check:
c = 3e8
f0 = 10.525e9
lam = c / f0
v = 100 / 3.6
fd = 2 * v / lam
R = 150
df = 100e6
Tm = 1e-3
fb = 2 * R * df / (c * Tm)
print(round(lam, 4))
print(round(fd))
print(round(fb))

traps: Using f<sub>d</sub> = v<sub>r</sub>/λ and losing the factor 2. The wave is shifted once going out and once coming back, so every speed reading is halved.
Putting km/h straight into 2v/λ. Convert to m/s first; 100 km/h is 27.78 m/s, not 100.
Using the total speed of the car instead of the radial component. A car crossing the beam has v<sub>r</sub> = v cos θ, and its Doppler shift falls as it turns.
In FMCW, using the carrier f<sub>0</sub> in place of the sweep bandwidth Δf. The beat frequency comes from the sweep, not from the carrier.
Forgetting that a plain CW radar cannot see a stationary target and cannot measure range, even if the Doppler frequency is measured perfectly.

quiz.q: State the Doppler formula for a radar and the sign convention for v<sub>r</sub>.
quiz.a: f<sub>d</sub> = 2v<sub>r</sub>/λ. v<sub>r</sub> is positive when the target is closing, so a closing target gives a positive f<sub>d</sub>; an opening target gives a negative f<sub>d</sub>.

quiz.q: Why can a single-frequency CW radar measure speed but not range?
quiz.a: It has no pulse or timing mark. The echo differs from the transmitter only in frequency, and that difference gives radial speed. Range needs a delay measurement or a frequency sweep.

quiz.q: A CW radar at 5.8 GHz sees a car opening at 54 km/h. Find the Doppler frequency, with sign.
quiz.a: v<sub>r</sub> = 54/3.6 = 15 m/s. λ = 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> / (5.8 × 10<sup>9</sup>) = 0.05172 m. f<sub>d</sub> = 2 × 15 / 0.05172 = 580 Hz. Opening, so f<sub>d</sub> = -580 Hz if closing is positive.

quiz.q: A CW radar at 10 GHz sees two cars approaching at 60 km/h, one at 20 m and one at 60 m. What does the Doppler spectrum show, and what change fixes the problem?
quiz.a: Both cars have the same radial speed, so both produce one Doppler line at the same f<sub>d</sub>; range is absent. Use FMCW or a pulse radar to add range, or use multiple tones to get phase range.

quiz.q: An FMCW radar has Δf = 200 MHz and T<sub>m</sub> = 2 ms. Find f<sub>b</sub> for R = 60 m and the range resolution.
Why does a CW radar often use separate transmit and receive antennas?
quiz.a: The transmitter runs continuously. Separate antennas give isolation so the strong transmit signal does not saturate or damage the receiver. A single antenna would need a circulator and would still leak.

quiz.q: How does triangular FMCW modulation separate range from Doppler shift?
quiz.a: The up-ramp and down-ramp give beats f<sub>b,up</sub> = f<sub>R</sub> - f<sub>d</sub> and f<sub>b,down</sub> = f<sub>R</sub> + f<sub>d</sub> (signs depend on sweep direction). Their average gives f<sub>R</sub>, hence range; their difference gives f<sub>d</sub>, hence radial speed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Automotive radar at 77 GHz uses FMCW with several receive antennas, and a two-dimensional FFT turns beat frequency into range and phase change between sweeps into speed. MIMO FMCW adds angle. Search for "range-Doppler FFT" and "FMCW MIMO radar" if you want the signal-processing side.
